quiz.q: Burning 1 kg of jet fuel makes about…
quiz.why: The fuel’s carbon combines with oxygen from the air.

quiz.q: NASA’s three paths to sustainable aviation are…
quiz.why: As listed by NASA.
opts: efficient aircraft, SAF, operations and infrastructure

quiz.q: If L/D rises 10%, fuel for the same trip falls roughly…
quiz.why: Fuel ∝ 1/(L/D).

quiz.q: U.S. aircraft covered by EPA’s rule emit what share of total U.S. greenhouse gases?
quiz.why: EPA: 3% of the national total.

quiz.q: Sustainable aviation fuel emits no CO₂ when burned.
quiz.why: It emits CO₂ like jet fuel; the benefit is that its carbon came recently from the air, so lifecycle emissions are lower.

quiz.q: Electric airplanes will soon replace all jets.
quiz.why: Battery energy density limits them to short, small flights for now.

quiz.q: Space is too big to pollute.
quiz.why: Debris in popular orbits is a real hazard.

quiz.q: Where does 3.16 come from? Model jet fuel as C₁₂H₂₃ and find kg of CO₂ per kg of fuel.
quiz.why: ≈ 3.16 kg of CO₂ per kg of fuel.

quiz.q: NASA estimates 620 million tonnes of fuel in 2050 at today’s efficiency. How much CO₂ is that?
quiz.why: ≈ 1,959 million tonnes, matching NASA’s “close to 2,000 megatons.”

quiz.q: A flight burns 5,000 kg of fuel. How much CO₂?
About 15%, since CO₂ is proportional to fuel burned.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit. If engines become 15% more fuel-efficient, by about how much do CO₂ emissions per trip fall?

quiz.q: Their energy per kilogram is far below jet fuel, and the Breguet trade makes extra weight very costly.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit. Why can’t today’s batteries power long-haul airliners?

quiz.q: ≈ 2.1 t of fuel and ≈ 6.7 t of CO₂ per flight (a simplified estimate).
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit. A flight burns 20 t of fuel. A new wing raises L/D from 17 to 19. Estimate the fuel and CO₂ saved.

quiz.q: This unit is the course’s planet tie-in in full: each equation from Units 3–7 is a lever on fuel burn, and fuel burn is CO₂. Engineers who can run these numbers design the cleaner aircraft that NASA and industry are working toward.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit.

quiz.q: EPA reports that the aircraft covered by its rule produce 10% of U.S. transportation greenhouse gas emissions, and NASA notes the U.S. committed in 2021 to net-zero aviation greenhouse gas emissions by 2050.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit.

quiz.q: Burning one kilogram of kerosene-type jet fuel produces about 3.16 kg of CO₂, fixed by chemistry. The only ways to cut it are to burn less fuel or to use fuel whose carbon came recently from the air.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit.

quiz.q: EPA reports that the aircraft covered by its greenhouse gas rule account for 10% of U.S. transportation greenhouse gas emissions and 3% of the U.S. total.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit.

quiz.q: NASA’s three paths: efficient aircraft technology, sustainable aviation fuel, and better operations and infrastructure.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit.

quiz.q: Today’s batteries store far less energy per kilogram than jet fuel, so electric aircraft suit short, small flights; hydrogen stores a lot of energy per kilogram but needs large tanks.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit.

quiz.q: Space sustainability means planning disposal so useful orbits stay open for the satellites that monitor Earth.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit.
